key_points: An extended ACL entry can match protocol, source address and wildcard, destination address and wildcard, and optional port numbers (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).
A wildcard mask is the inverse of a subnet mask: a 0 bit means the address bit must match, and a 1 bit means it is ignored.
Port operators such as eq, gt, lt, and range apply only when the protocol is TCP or UDP.
Numbered extended IP ACLs use 100-199 and 2000-2699, and named extended ACLs use ip access-list extended.
Every ACL ends with an implicit deny any, so traffic not matched by a permit statement is dropped.
guide.explanation: Extended ACLs filter traffic using more fields than standard ACLs, including protocol, source, destination, and port. Each entry is read in order, and the first match decides whether the packet is permitted or denied (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management). Wildcard masks tell the router which address bits to compare, and port numbers narrow the match to a specific service.
guide.example: For the network 10.0.0.0/24, the subnet mask $255.255.255.0$ inverts to the wildcard $0.0.0.255$. The entry access-list 101 deny tcp 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.5.20 eq 23 blocks TCP port 23 (Telnet) from that network to host 192.168.5.20 and leaves other traffic to be checked by later entries (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: In the entry access-list 110 permit tcp any any eq 443, what does eq 443 match?
questions.explanation: The port operand follows the destination specification (the second any), so it matches the destination TCP port 443 (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: What is the wildcard mask for the subnet mask 255.255.255.0?
questions.explanation: Inverting each octet of 255.255.255.0 gives 0.0.0.255, so the first three octets must match and the last octet is ignored (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: What is the wildcard mask for the network 172.16.8.0/21?
questions.explanation: A /21 subnet mask is 255.255.248.0. Inverting 248 (11111000) gives 7 (00000111), so the wildcard is 0.0.7.255 (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: Which access-list number range identifies numbered extended IP ACLs?
questions.explanation: Numbers 100-199 (and 2000-2699) are used for extended IP ACLs, while 1-99 identifies standard IP ACLs (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: Which command starts a named extended ACL called BLOCK-TELNET?
questions.explanation: The ip access-list extended name command creates a named extended ACL and enters its configuration mode (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: Which protocol keyword should be used to filter DNS queries that use UDP port 53?
questions.explanation: DNS queries normally use UDP port 53, so the udp keyword is needed before the port operand. Port operators apply only to TCP and UDP (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: What does the entry access-list 101 deny tcp 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.5.20 eq 23 block?
options: All IP traffic from 10.0.0.0/24 to any host
questions.explanation: The source is 10.0.0.0 with wildcard 0.0.0.255 (a /24 network), the destination is host 192.168.5.20, and eq 23 matches TCP port 23, which is Telnet (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: Which field can an extended ACL match that a standard ACL cannot?
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs match only the source address, while extended ACLs can also match the destination address, protocol, and port numbers (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: What wildcard mask matches only the single host 10.1.1.5?
questions.explanation: A wildcard of 0.0.0.0 requires every bit to match exactly, which selects only one address. The host keyword is an equivalent shortcut (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).

questions.question: Which rule applies to traffic that does not match any entry in an ACL?
options: The implicit deny any at the end is applied
The implicit permit any at the end is applied
The traffic is forwarded to the default gateway
The traffic is sent to the syslog server
questions.answer: The implicit deny any at the end is applied
questions.explanation: Every ACL has an implicit deny any statement at the end, so unmatched traffic is dropped. This is why at least one permit entry is needed when other traffic must pass (Outline week 7: Extended ACLs + Network Management).
